💬 Pezeshkian urges int’l support for countries facing environmental costs of war, sanctions

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has reaffirmed the country’s commitment to biodiversity conservation, urging the international community to ensure that countries facing sanctions or military aggression do not bear the environmental costs alone.

Addressing the Leaders’ Summit of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, held as part of COP 17 in Armenia’s Yerevan on Friday, Pezeshkian condemned the devastating impact of wars of aggression on nature, describing it as “ecocide,” and called on the international community to establish effective, transparent, and enforceable mechanisms to protect natural heritage and biodiversity during wartime.
​
He said war not only kills people and destroys economic infrastructure but also burns forests, damages wetlands, contaminates soil, threatens water resources and destroys wildlife habitats. He warned that such damage can persist for years or even generations after hostilities end.
​
The president stressed that the environmental consequences of the US and Israeli regimes’ war of aggression in the region, including Iran, underscore the need for greater international attention to the ecological impacts of armed conflicts. Damage to industrial and energy facilities, water and soil pollution, and threats to ecosystems and biodiversity conservation infrastructure have all contributed to these concerns, he added.
​
Pezeshkian said these consequences are not confined to individual countries or their political borders, emphasizing that nature recognizes no political boundaries and that water, soil, and air pollution do not stop at national borders. Therefore, the environmental damage caused by war is a global issue requiring international solutions, he added.
​
He called on the international community to establish effective, transparent, and enforceable mechanisms to protect natural heritage and biodiversity, stressing that nature must not be treated as a “silent and defenseless victim” of war.
​
The president also said countries under economic sanctions or exposed to military aggression should not be left to bear alone the environmental costs of sanctions or wars they did not initiate.
​
He urged international organizations to strengthen funding mechanisms, environmental damage assessments, ecosystem restoration efforts, and support for affected countries to address the environmental consequences of armed conflicts.
​
Pezeshkian reaffirmed Iran’s readiness to share its scientific expertise, academic capabilities, and experience with other countries, describing biodiversity conservation as an important avenue for “peace diplomacy.”
​
He noted that the region faces multiple challenges, including security crises stemming from the unlawful and expansionist presence of powers, climate change, water scarcity, and ecosystem degradation. Environmental cooperation, he said, could help build bridges between nations and pave the way for peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future in harmony with the natural world.
​
The Leaders’ Summit, held in Yerevan on Friday, brings together heads of state and government, leaders of international organizations, globally recognized scientists, prominent cultural figures, representatives of indigenous peoples and local communities and other key stakeholders. Under the motto “Leaders’ for Nature,” the summit serves as the political anchor for the Conference of the Parties (COP 17).

One of the key moments when I truly understood how transformers work: 🧠✨

"Stop thinking of a transformer as a conveyor belt, where each layer transforms the output of the previous one."

"Start thinking of it as a residual flow." 🌊

Each block in a transformer has a residual connection that adds the input of the block to its output:

x' = f(x) + x

Because of this addition, the attention mechanism or MLP within the layer – the function f in the formula above – actually does NOT transform the input. Instead, it calculates the information that needs to be ADDED to the input before passing it to the next block! ➕

Imagine the main part of the transformer as a shared whiteboard. 📝 Each block reads what it needs from it and adds its own notes. All changes are additions.

Furthermore, layers can exchange information over distances. A block in the first layer can write information, and a block in the fifth layer can read it, even though there is no direct connection between them. 🔗

I owe these ideas to an older article by Anthropic about the architecture of transformers:
transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework
